narrative:
After carefully reviewing your application, the admissions process — which uses a predictive model to assess bar exam readiness — determined that your profile carries a 51.8% likelihood of not passing the bar exam on the first attempt. While this is a narrow margin, it was sufficient to result in a rejection, as the threshold for admission requires a stronger confidence in first-time bar passage. Understanding exactly why this outcome was reached can help you take meaningful steps forward.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your academic performance during your third year of law school, specifically the decile ranking you achieved relative to your classmates. You placed in the 1st decile in Year 3, meaning your grades ranked among the lowest 10% of students in your school at that stage. Among students who successfully passed the bar exam, the average third-year decile ranking was nearly 6 out of 10 — a striking contrast that weighed heavily against your application. This factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward a projected failure, and it reflects a concern that your academic trajectory in the later, more advanced stages of legal study may not have built the depth of knowledge the bar exam demands.

Your first-year academic standing told a similar story, though it was not among the top three most influential factors in the model's final assessment. You ranked in the 2nd decile in Year 1, again well below the average of approximately 6 among students who passed, suggesting that the academic challenges were present from early on in your legal education.

On a more encouraging note, two factors actually worked in your favor. Your LSAT score of 36, while slightly below the average of 37.27 among students who passed, still contributed modestly toward a more positive prediction — meaning it nudged the model in the direction of passing, even if only partially. More notably, your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 is actually above the average of 3.24 among students who passed, and this too pushed the prediction in a favorable direction. These strengths signal that your foundational academic abilities and pre-law preparation are genuine assets.

As a full-time student, you are already positioned similarly to the vast majority of successful bar passers, over 93% of whom studied full-time, so your commitment and availability for rigorous study are not in question. Given all of this, the most actionable path forward is to focus intensively on strengthening your law school academic performance, particularly in your upper-level coursework, as this appears to be the clearest gap between your current profile and those of students who succeed on the bar exam. Consider seeking academic support resources, study groups, or tutoring in areas where your grades have struggled, and speak with your academic advisor about strategies to improve your class standing before reapplying.
